title: Nose, Sinus, Throat and Airway Disorders
summary: Learn common and dangerous conditions of the nose, sinuses, pharynx and larynx.

lessons.title: Epistaxis: Anterior vs Posterior Bleeds

levels.kid:
A nosebleed happens when tiny blood tubes inside your nose break. These tubes sit very close to the surface, like thin threads just under wet paper. Dry air, picking, or a bump can tear them.

Most nosebleeds come from the **front** of the nose. They look scary but usually stop on their own with the right help.

Here is what to do:
- Sit up and lean **forward**, not back, so blood does not run down your throat.
- Pinch the soft part of your nose firmly.
- Keep pinching for about 10 to 15 minutes without peeking.

A few nosebleeds come from far in the **back** of the nose. Those are rarer and often happen in older people. They need a doctor's help to stop.
levels.hs:
**Epistaxis** is the medical word for a nosebleed. It is very common: about 60% of people have one in their lifetime, but only a small fraction need a doctor.

Doctors split nosebleeds into two types:
- **Anterior bleeds** (about 90%) come from the front of the nasal septum, the wall dividing the two nostrils. Here several arteries join in a network called **Kiesselbach's plexus** (also called Little's area). The lining is thin and exposed to dry air and fingers, so it bleeds easily. These are common in children.
- **Posterior bleeds** (about 10%) come from deep in the nose, mostly from branches of the **sphenopalatine artery**. They are heavier, often drain down the throat, and are more common in older adults with high blood pressure or on blood-thinning medicines.

Common causes include dry air, nose picking, colds and allergies, injury, and nasal sprays. Medicines that thin the blood, such as aspirin or warfarin, make bleeds harder to stop.

First aid is simple: sit up, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10 to 15 minutes. Leaning back is a myth that just makes you swallow blood.

Example: a 7-year-old who gets nosebleeds every winter, usually from one side, almost certainly has an anterior bleed from Kiesselbach's plexus.
levels.college:
**Vascular anatomy** explains the anterior/posterior split. The nose is supplied by both carotid systems:
- **External carotid**: the **sphenopalatine artery** (terminal branch of the maxillary artery) supplies most of the posterior septum and lateral wall; the **greater palatine** and **superior labial** (from the facial artery) supply the anterior floor and septum.
- **Internal carotid**: the **anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries** (from the ophthalmic artery) supply the superior nasal cavity.

**Kiesselbach's plexus** on the anterior septum is where the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine (septal branch), greater palatine and superior labial arteries meet. It is the source of about 90% of bleeds. **Woodruff's plexus**, a venous plexus on the posterior lateral wall, is a traditional source of posterior bleeds, which are mostly arterial from sphenopalatine branches.

**Causes**
- Local: digital trauma, dry mucosa, infection, septal deviation or perforation, intranasal steroid sprays, fractures, tumors.
- Systemic: anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs, coagulopathies (von Willebrand disease, hemophilia), liver disease, **hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT)**.

**Stepwise management**
- Assess airway and circulation. Brisk bleeding may need resuscitation.
- Firm pressure on the soft nose for 10 to 15 minutes, patient leaning forward.
- **Topical vasoconstrictor** (oxymetazoline) and local anesthetic, then inspect with a nasal speculum and headlight.
- **Cautery** of a visible anterior vessel, usually with silver nitrate, on one side of the septum at a time to avoid perforation.
- **Anterior packing** (expandable sponge, gauze or balloon) if cautery fails; **tranexamic acid** is often applied topically.
- If blood keeps flowing into the pharynx despite good anterior packing, suspect a **posterior bleed**: place a posterior balloon or Foley catheter with anterior pack, admit, and involve ENT.

Posterior packing is uncomfortable and can cause hypoxia and vagal responses, so these patients are monitored as inpatients.
levels.phd:
Epistaxis epidemiology is bimodal, peaking in children under 10 and adults over 50, with a winter excess linked to low humidity and upper respiratory infections. Anterior bleeds arise from Kiesselbach's plexus, where submucosal arterioles lie beneath a thin, minimally cushioned mucosa over septal cartilage. Drying causes crusting and fissuring, and removing crusts re-tears healing vessels, which keeps the cycle going.

**Hypertension** is the classic association with posterior bleeds, but causality is debated. Patients are often hypertensive *during* a bleed because of anxiety and pain, and cross-sectional studies conflict. Long-standing hypertension may cause vessel wall fibrosis that impairs vasoconstriction, prolonging rather than starting bleeds. Current guidance (the AAO-HNS 2020 Clinical Practice Guideline on Nosebleed) advises against routinely lowering blood pressure acutely to control a bleed, while recommending that it be monitored.

**Antithrombotic therapy** is the dominant modern risk factor. Antiplatelet agents, warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) increase recurrence and hospitalization, but the guideline advises against stopping them in most cases unless bleeding is life-threatening, because thrombotic risk usually outweighs the benefit.

**Tranexamic acid (TXA)**, a lysine analogue, blocks plasminogen's lysine-binding sites and so inhibits fibrinolysis. Trial evidence is mixed. Early emergency department trials of topical TXA suggested faster control and less packing, but the large UK **NoPAC trial** (Reuben et al., 2021) found that intravenous TXA did not reduce the need for anterior packing. Topical use remains common.

**HHT** (Osler-Weber-Rendu) is autosomal dominant, caused by mutations in *ENG* (HHT1), *ACVRL1/ALK1* (HHT2) or *SMAD4*, all in the TGF-beta/BMP9 signaling pathway. Defective signaling produces fragile telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations. Recurrent epistaxis is the most common symptom, and the Curaçao criteria (epistaxis, telangiectasias, visceral AVMs, family history) define the diagnosis.
levels.expert:
Recurrent or refractory posterior epistaxis has moved from prolonged packing toward early definitive intervention. **Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation (ESPAL)** reaches the artery as it exits the sphenopalatine foramen, behind the **crista ethmoidalis**, a key landmark. Reported success rates are about 85% to 98%. Several cohorts suggest it costs less and shortens admission compared with packing for 48 to 72 hours, so many centers offer it early. Missing accessory branches, which commonly exit through separate foramina, is a classic cause of failure. If bleeding persists, consider anterior ethmoidal artery ligation, through an external Lynch incision or endoscopically.

**Endovascular embolization** of internal maxillary and facial artery branches is an alternative with comparable efficacy. It carries particular risks: stroke, facial nerve palsy, facial pain and skin necrosis. Danger lies in external-to-internal carotid anastomoses, such as the ophthalmic and middle meningeal connections. Ethmoidal bleeding cannot be safely embolized because it comes from the ophthalmic artery, so a superior source favors surgery.

**Pitfalls worth knowing:**
- Unilateral epistaxis with obstruction in an **adolescent male** suggests **juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma**. It arises near the sphenopalatine foramen and must not be biopsied in clinic because it is highly vascular. Imaging comes first, and treatment is often preoperative embolization and endoscopic resection.
- In adults, unilateral bleeding with crusting or obstruction warrants endoscopy to exclude sinonasal malignancy.
- Delayed, torrential epistaxis weeks after head trauma or skull base surgery suggests **traumatic internal carotid pseudoaneurysm**, which is managed endovascularly and can be fatal.
- Toxic shock syndrome is a rare complication of packing. Prophylactic antibiotics are of uncertain value and guidelines do not routinely recommend them.

For **HHT**, management increasingly targets the vascular biology. Systemic **bevacizumab** (anti-VEGF) reduces bleeding and transfusion needs. The 2020 international HHT guidelines endorse topical/oral TXA, laser photocoagulation and systemic antiangiogenics. Pomalidomide showed benefit in the PATH-HHT trial. Septodermoplasty and Young's procedure (nostril closure) are reserved for severe disease. Open questions include durable antiangiogenic regimens and whether pathway-specific therapies can restore BMP9/ALK1 signaling.

keyPoints: About 90% of nosebleeds are anterior, from Kiesselbach's plexus on the septum
Posterior bleeds mostly come from the sphenopalatine artery and are heavier
First aid: lean forward and pinch the soft nose for 10-15 minutes
Escalate from pressure and vasoconstrictor to cautery, packing, then posterior balloon
Anticoagulants, coagulopathy and HHT make bleeds harder to stop
Refractory posterior bleeds: endoscopic sphenopalatine ligation or embolization

test.q: Roughly what share of nosebleeds are anterior?
test.explain: About 90% of nosebleeds arise anteriorly, mostly from Kiesselbach's plexus.

test.q: Kiesselbach's plexus is located on the:
test.explain: It sits on the front of the septum. Woodruff's plexus is on the posterior lateral wall.

test.q: Which artery is the main source of posterior epistaxis?
test.explain: The sphenopalatine artery, the terminal branch of the maxillary artery, supplies the posterior nasal cavity.

test.q: Correct first aid for a nosebleed is to:
choices: Tilt the head back and pinch the bony bridge
Lean forward and pinch the soft nose
Blow the nose hard to clear clots
Lie flat with an ice pack on the neck
test.explain: Leaning forward stops swallowing of blood, and pinching the soft part compresses Kiesselbach's plexus. Tilting back is a myth.

test.q: The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries branch from the:
test.explain: The ethmoidal arteries come from the ophthalmic artery, part of the internal carotid system.

test.q: Why is septal cautery done on one side at a time?
choices: To keep the patient from fainting
To let the silver nitrate dry first
To protect nearby branches of the facial nerve
To lower the risk of septal perforation
test.explain: Cauterizing both sides of the septum at once can damage its blood supply and cause a perforation.

test.q: Blood keeps running down the throat despite a well-placed anterior pack. This suggests:
test.explain: Continued bleeding into the pharynx after good anterior packing points to a posterior source.

test.q: Which group is most typical for posterior epistaxis?
choices: Young athletes after a light bump
test.explain: Posterior bleeds are more common in older adults, especially with hypertension or antithrombotic drugs.

test.q: Tranexamic acid helps control bleeding by:
test.explain: TXA blocks plasminogen's lysine-binding sites, so clots are broken down more slowly.

test.q: What is the medical term for a nosebleed?
test.explain: Epistaxis is the term for bleeding from the nose.

test.q: Little's area is another name for ___ plexus.
test.explain: Little's area and Kiesselbach's plexus are the same anterior septal region.

test.q: Hereditary hemorrhagic ___ is a genetic cause of recurrent nosebleeds.
test.explain: HHT causes fragile telangiectasias in the nose, so recurrent epistaxis is its most common symptom.

kidTest.q: Where do most nosebleeds come from?
kidTest.explain: Most nosebleeds start in the front, where tiny blood tubes sit close to the surface.

kidTest.q: Which way should you lean during a nosebleed?
kidTest.explain: Leaning forward keeps blood from running down your throat.

kidTest.q: Which part of the nose should you pinch?
kidTest.explain: Pinching the soft part presses on the bleeding spot.

kidTest.q: Who has back-of-the-nose bleeds more often?
kidTest.explain: Bleeds from the back of the nose are rarer and happen more in older people.

kidTest.q: Dry ___ can make tiny nose blood tubes crack. (a _ _)
kidTest.explain: Dry air dries the inside of the nose so it cracks and bleeds.

advancedTest.q: A superior nasal cavity bleed persists after sphenopalatine ligation. Why is embolization a poor next step?
choices: Ethmoidal arteries come from the ophthalmic artery, risking vision loss
Embolization works for venous bleeds but not for these small arterial ones
The maxillary artery is hard to reach by catheter once it has been ligated
Tranexamic acid given earlier makes the embolic material less effective
advancedTest.explain: The ethmoidal supply comes from the internal carotid via the ophthalmic artery, so embolizing it threatens the retina. Surgical ethmoidal ligation is preferred.

advancedTest.q: A patient arrives bleeding with a very high blood pressure. Which interpretation best fits current evidence?
choices: High pressure means anticoagulants should be stopped at once
High pressure rules out a posterior bleed and points to an anterior one
High pressure proves hypertension started the bleed, so lower it fast
The high reading may partly reflect anxiety, so monitor it rather than lower it acutely
advancedTest.explain: Causality is debated, and acute readings are inflated by anxiety and pain. The 2020 guideline advises monitoring rather than routine acute lowering.

advancedTest.q: A 15-year-old boy has repeated one-sided nosebleeds and nasal blockage. What is the key safety point?
choices: Image first and avoid biopsy in clinic
Cauterize the mass in clinic and send him home
Assume Kiesselbach's plexus and teach first aid
Pack both sides and start long-term antibiotics
advancedTest.explain: This picture suggests juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, which is highly vascular. Biopsy can cause severe bleeding, so imaging comes first.

advancedTest.q: Why do antiangiogenic drugs such as bevacizumab make sense in HHT?
choices: They counter VEGF-driven vessel growth from faulty BMP9 signaling
They permanently constrict the sphenopalatine artery and its branches
They kill the bacteria that inflame and crust the nasal lining
They boost the liver's production of clotting factors such as factor VIII
advancedTest.explain: HHT mutations disrupt TGF-beta/BMP9 signaling, which leads to fragile, VEGF-driven abnormal vessels. Anti-VEGF therapy targets this underlying biology.

lessons.title: Rhinosinusitis and Its Orbital and Intracranial Complications

levels.kid:
Inside your face are hollow spaces filled with air, called **sinuses**. They sit around your nose, under your eyes and above your eyebrows. They have little doors that let mucus drain into your nose.

When you have a cold, those doors can get puffy and blocked. Mucus gets stuck, your face feels full, and your nose runs. That is **sinusitis**. Most of the time it goes away by itself, just like a cold.

The eye sits right next to a sinus, with only a very thin bone wall between them. Very rarely, a germ sneaks through that wall. Then the eye gets swollen and red, and it hurts to move. That needs a doctor fast, because the eye and brain are close neighbors.
levels.hs:
The **paranasal sinuses** are air-filled spaces in the skull bones: the maxillary sinuses (cheeks), the ethmoid sinuses (between the eyes), the frontal sinuses (forehead) and the sphenoid sinus (deep behind the nose). They are lined with mucus-making tissue. Tiny hairs called **cilia** sweep mucus out through small drainage openings.

**Rhinosinusitis** means inflammation of the nose and sinuses. It is called **acute** if it lasts under 4 weeks and **chronic** if it lasts 12 weeks or more. Main symptoms are a blocked nose, discolored discharge, facial pain or pressure, and a reduced sense of smell.

Most acute cases are caused by **viruses**, the same ones behind colds, and they get better in about 7 to 10 days. A bacterial infection is more likely if symptoms last more than 10 days, are severe, or get better and then get worse again ("double worsening").

Complications are rare but serious. The ethmoid sinuses are separated from the eye socket by a paper-thin bone, the **lamina papyracea**. Infection can spread through it into the orbit. Example: a child with a cold develops a swollen eyelid, then a bulging eye, pain on eye movement and blurry vision. That is **orbital cellulitis**, an emergency. Frontal sinus infection can also spread to the brain, causing **meningitis** or a **brain abscess**.
levels.college:
**Definitions (adult guidelines, e.g., EPOS 2020, AAO-HNS 2015):** rhinosinusitis requires two or more symptoms, one of which is nasal blockage or discharge, with or without facial pain/pressure or loss of smell. It is **acute (ARS)** under 4 weeks and **chronic (CRS)** at 12 weeks or more, with or without nasal polyps.

**Pathophysiology.** Sinuses drain through narrow ostia. The maxillary, anterior ethmoid and frontal sinuses drain to the **ostiomeatal complex** in the middle meatus. Mucosal swelling blocks the ostia, so mucociliary clearance fails, oxygen tension falls and secretions stagnate. These conditions favor bacterial overgrowth.

**Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS)** follows only about 0.5 to 2% of viral episodes. Typical organisms are *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae* and *Moraxella catarrhalis*. Clues to ABRS: symptoms lasting over 10 days without improvement, high fever with purulent discharge, or double worsening.

**Orbital complications: the Chandler classification**
- I: preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis, in front of the orbital septum
- II: orbital cellulitis, behind the septum
- III: subperiosteal abscess, usually medial, next to the ethmoids
- IV: orbital abscess
- V: cavernous sinus thrombosis

The danger signs that separate postseptal from preseptal disease are **proptosis, ophthalmoplegia or pain on eye movement, reduced acuity, impaired color vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect**.

**Intracranial complications** come mainly from frontal sinusitis, typically in adolescent males. They include epidural and subdural empyema, meningitis, brain abscess and venous sinus thrombosis. Spread occurs through valveless diploic veins and through bone erosion. **Pott's puffy tumor** is a frontal subperiosteal abscess with osteomyelitis and is often linked to intracranial spread.

**Imaging:** contrast CT of the sinuses and orbits. MRI is added when intracranial disease is suspected.
levels.phd:
**Mucosal biology.** The sinonasal epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. Its cilia beat at about 10 to 15 Hz and move mucus along fixed pathways toward the natural ostia, whatever surgical openings exist. This explains why surgery aims to restore natural drainage pathways rather than create new holes. Nasal nitric oxide is high and is produced largely by the sinuses. It is antimicrobial and stimulates ciliary beating, and it is markedly low in primary ciliary dyskinesia.

**CRS endotypes.** Chronic rhinosinusitis is no longer treated as one disease. **Type 2 inflammation** (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, eosinophils, periostin, local IgE) dominates CRS with nasal polyps in Western populations. Type 1 and type 3 (IL-17, neutrophilic) profiles are more frequent in CRS without polyps and in East Asian polyp disease. Other features include *Staphylococcus aureus* enterotoxins acting as superantigens, biofilms, and epithelial barrier defects such as reduced tight-junction proteins and high TSLP and IL-33. **Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease** links polyps, asthma and COX-1 inhibitor sensitivity. Its mechanism is dysregulated arachidonic acid metabolism, with leukotriene overproduction and low PGE2.

**Routes of complication spread**
- **Orbit:** contiguous spread through the lamina papyracea and its dehiscences. Ethmoid foramina carry neurovascular bundles. The orbital veins are valveless and connect to the cavernous sinus.
- **Cranium:** diploic veins of Breschet in the frontal bone are valveless and allow retrograde thrombophlebitis. Direct erosion of the posterior frontal table can also seed the epidural or subdural space.

**Microbiology of complications** shifts toward the *Streptococcus anginosus* (milleri) group, anaerobes and *S. aureus*, including MRSA. *S. anginosus* is notably abscess-forming and is strongly associated with intracranial suppuration.

**Chandler (1970)** described spatial stages rather than a strict time sequence. Patients can present at any stage. Many children with small medial subperiosteal abscesses recover with intravenous antibiotics alone. Garcia and Harris proposed criteria for this approach: age under 9, medial location, modest abscess size, intact vision and no frontal involvement.

**Controversy:** CT findings correlate poorly with symptoms in CRS. Lund-Mackay scores of a few points occur in asymptomatic people, so imaging cannot diagnose CRS on its own.
levels.expert:
**Clinical pitfalls in the swollen eye.** Gross eyelid edema can mask proptosis and restricted eye movement. Retract the lids, check acuity and red desaturation, and test for an RAPD at every review. Decline in optic nerve function, or orbital compartment syndrome, may require urgent drainage or lateral canthotomy and cantholysis whatever the imaging shows. Bilateral signs, a cranial nerve III, IV or VI palsy, V1/V2 numbness or a septic picture suggest **cavernous sinus thrombosis**. MR venography or contrast-enhanced MRI is the test. Anticoagulation remains debated but is increasingly used.

**Management principles.** Treat with intravenous broad-spectrum therapy that covers streptococci, staphylococci and anaerobes, with nasal decongestion. Endoscopic sinus surgery with external or endoscopic drainage is indicated for abscesses failing medical therapy, large or non-medial collections, or vision loss. Multidisciplinary care with ophthalmology, neurosurgery and infectious diseases is the norm.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Subdural empyema progresses fast and can appear small on CT. Its tell-tale features are seizures, hemiparesis and declining consciousness in an adolescent with frontal sinusitis. **MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging is superior to CT**, because pus restricts diffusion. Treatment is usually urgent evacuation, often by craniotomy rather than burr holes for subdural collections, together with sinus drainage in the same session. Several series noted a rise in pediatric intracranial complications after 2020, with *S. anginosus* prominent. Whether this reflects changes in viral circulation or other causes is still unclear.

**Invasive fungal sinusitis** must be distinguished early. **Acute invasive** disease (Mucorales, *Aspergillus*) occurs in neutropenia, diabetic ketoacidosis and transplant recipients. It causes black or insensate mucosa, rapid orbital apex syndrome and carotid involvement. Mucormycosis surged in India during COVID-19, linked to steroids and uncontrolled diabetes. Treatment combines amphotericin-based therapy, reversal of the underlying immunosuppression and radical debridement.

**Frontiers in CRS with nasal polyps.** Biologics have changed refractory disease: **dupilumab** (IL-4Rα), **omalizumab** (IgE) and **mepolizumab** (IL-5). Open questions include how to choose between surgery and a biologic, which biomarkers to use (tissue eosinophils, blood eosinophils, IgE), long-term cost, and newer agents such as tezepelumab (anti-TSLP).

keyPoints: Acute rhinosinusitis lasts under 4 weeks; chronic lasts 12 weeks or more
Most acute cases are viral; suspect bacteria if over 10 days, severe, or double worsening
Thin lamina papyracea lets ethmoid infection spread into the orbit
Chandler stages: preseptal, orbital cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess, orbital abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis
Proptosis, painful eye movement, vision loss or RAPD mean postseptal emergency
Frontal sinusitis can spread via valveless diploic veins to cause empyema and brain abscess

test.q: Chronic rhinosinusitis is defined by symptoms lasting at least:
test.explain: Chronic means 12 weeks or more. Acute disease lasts under 4 weeks.

test.q: What causes most cases of acute rhinosinusitis?
test.explain: Most acute episodes are viral, and only about 0.5 to 2% become bacterial.

test.q: Which feature most suggests acute bacterial rather than viral sinusitis?
choices: Clear runny nose on day two
A sore throat at the onset
test.explain: Double worsening, symptoms lasting over 10 days, or severe onset point to a bacterial infection.

test.q: Infection from which sinus most commonly spreads into the orbit?
test.explain: The ethmoid sinuses sit next to the orbit, behind the paper-thin lamina papyracea.

test.q: Which finding indicates infection behind the orbital septum?
test.explain: Pain on eye movement or restricted movement, proptosis and vision changes signal postseptal (orbital) disease. Eyelid swelling alone can be preseptal.

test.q: In the Chandler classification, stage V is:
test.explain: The order is preseptal, orbital cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess, orbital abscess, then cavernous sinus thrombosis.

test.q: Intracranial complications most often arise from which sinus?
test.explain: Frontal sinusitis, typically in adolescent males, spreads through diploic veins or bone erosion.

test.q: Pott's puffy tumor is a:
choices: Benign bony growth in the nose
Nasal polyp in the maxillary sinus
test.explain: It is a subperiosteal frontal abscess with osteomyelitis of the frontal bone, often linked to intracranial spread.

test.q: The usual first imaging test for suspected orbital complication is:
test.explain: Contrast CT of the sinuses and orbits shows sinus disease and orbital abscesses. MRI is added if intracranial spread is suspected.

test.q: The paper-thin bone between the ethmoid sinus and orbit is the lamina ___.
test.explain: Lamina papyracea means 'paper layer', and infection can cross it.

test.q: What are the tiny hairs that sweep mucus out of the sinuses called?
test.explain: Cilia drive mucociliary clearance toward the sinus openings.

test.q: The maxillary, anterior ethmoid and frontal sinuses drain into the ostiomeatal ___.
test.explain: The ostiomeatal complex in the middle meatus is the shared drainage pathway.

kidTest.q: What are sinuses?
kidTest.explain: Sinuses are hollow air spaces around your nose and eyes.

kidTest.q: What often starts sinusitis?
kidTest.explain: A cold can make the sinus doors puffy and blocked.

kidTest.q: What usually happens to sinusitis?
kidTest.explain: Most sinusitis gets better on its own, like a cold.

kidTest.q: Why does a swollen, painful eye need a doctor fast?
choices: The eye and brain are close
kidTest.explain: The infection is near the eye and brain, so it is serious.

kidTest.q: What gets stuck in blocked sinuses? (m _ _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: Mucus can't drain, so your face feels full.

advancedTest.q: Why does endoscopic sinus surgery aim to widen natural ostia rather than create new openings?
choices: New openings damage the sense of smell
New openings tend to heal closed within days
Natural ostia contain the immune cells
Cilia carry mucus toward natural ostia anyway
advancedTest.explain: Mucociliary flow follows fixed pathways to the natural ostia, so extra openings are bypassed.

advancedTest.q: An adolescent with frontal sinusitis has seizures and hemiparesis, but CT shows only a thin extra-axial collection. Best next step?
advancedTest.explain: Subdural empyema can look small on CT. Pus restricts diffusion on MRI, and the clinical picture demands urgent evaluation.

advancedTest.q: A child has a small medial subperiosteal abscess, normal vision and no frontal disease. What is most reasonable?
advancedTest.explain: Garcia-Harris-type criteria support trialing intravenous antibiotics alone, with surgery if the child fails to improve or vision declines.

advancedTest.q: A diabetic patient in ketoacidosis has black, numb nasal mucosa and rapid vision loss. Which process is most likely?
advancedTest.explain: Mucorales cause angioinvasive necrosis in ketoacidosis and need antifungals plus urgent debridement.

lessons.title: Pharyngitis, Peritonsillar Abscess and Tonsillectomy

levels.kid:
At the back of your mouth are two soft lumps called **tonsils**. They are like guards at a castle gate, catching germs that try to sneak in.

Sometimes the throat gets sore and red. That is called **pharyngitis**. Most of the time a virus causes it, the same kind that gives you a cold, and it gets better on its own. Sometimes a germ called **strep** causes it. Then a doctor can do a quick throat swab and give medicine that kills the germ.

Rarely, a pocket of pus forms next to a tonsil. It hurts a lot and makes it hard to open your mouth. Doctors drain it.

If tonsils cause trouble again and again, a surgeon can take them out. That is a **tonsillectomy**.
levels.hs:
**Pharyngitis** means inflammation of the pharynx, the tube behind the nose and mouth. It causes sore throat, pain on swallowing and often fever.

- **Viral pharyngitis** is the most common type. Clues include cough, runny nose, hoarseness and red eyes. Antibiotics do not help.
- **Bacterial pharyngitis** is most often caused by **group A Streptococcus** (*Streptococcus pyogenes*), called "strep throat." It is most common in children aged 5 to 15. Clues include fever, swollen tender neck lymph nodes, white patches (**exudate**) on the tonsils and *no* cough.

Doctors confirm strep with a **rapid antigen test** or a **throat culture**. Strep is treated with antibiotics, usually penicillin or amoxicillin. One major reason is to prevent **rheumatic fever**, an immune reaction that can damage heart valves.

A **peritonsillar abscess** (also called **quinsy**) is a collection of pus between a tonsil and the muscle wall behind it. Warning signs include a "hot potato" muffled voice, trouble opening the mouth (**trismus**), drooling, and the uvula pushed to the opposite side. It needs drainage plus antibiotics.

A **tonsillectomy** is surgery to remove the palatine tonsils. A real example: a child with seven proven throat infections in one year, or loud snoring with pauses in breathing at night, may be offered tonsillectomy.
levels.college:
**Etiology of acute pharyngitis.** Most cases are viral (rhinovirus, adenovirus, coronaviruses, influenza). **Epstein-Barr virus** causes infectious mononucleosis: exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, fatigue and splenomegaly. Giving amoxicillin during EBV infection often produces a widespread rash. Group A Streptococcus (GAS) causes roughly 20 to 30% of pediatric sore throats but only about 5 to 15% in adults.

**Clinical scoring.** The **Centor criteria** give one point each for:
- Fever
- Tonsillar exudate
- Tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy
- Absence of cough

The **McIsaac modification** adds a point for age 3 to 14 and subtracts one for age 45 or over. Low scores need no testing. Intermediate scores warrant a rapid antigen detection test (RADT). In children, a negative RADT is backed up by culture because RADT sensitivity is imperfect and the risk of rheumatic fever is highest at these ages.

**Why treat GAS?** Antibiotics:
- prevent **acute rheumatic fever** (they are effective if started within about 9 days of symptom onset);
- reduce suppurative complications;
- shorten symptoms modestly and limit spread.

They do *not* reliably prevent **post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis**. Penicillin or amoxicillin is first line, because GAS has no documented penicillin resistance.

**Peritonsillar abscess (PTA).** This is the most common deep infection of the head and neck. It is usually polymicrobial (GAS, *Fusobacterium necrophorum*, oral anaerobes). Pus collects between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle, usually at the superior pole. Signs include unilateral bulging of the soft palate, uvular deviation away from the affected side, trismus from irritation of the medial pterygoid, and a muffled voice. Peritonsillar **cellulitis** has no drainable pus. Management is needle aspiration or incision and drainage, plus antibiotics with anaerobic coverage.

**Tonsillectomy** removes the palatine tonsils, usually with the adenoids in children. The main indications are recurrent throat infection and obstructive sleep-disordered breathing.
levels.phd:
**Group A streptococcal pathogenesis.** GAS virulence centers on the **M protein** (encoded by *emm*), which resists phagocytosis by binding factor H and fibrinogen and so limiting complement deposition. Its other virulence factors include the hyaluronic acid capsule, streptolysins O and S, and streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins, which act as superantigens. **Acute rheumatic fever** arises from **molecular mimicry**. Antibodies and T cells against M protein and the group A carbohydrate (N-acetylglucosamine) cross-react with cardiac myosin, laminin and valvular endothelium, which produces carditis and, over time, mitral-predominant valve disease. Classic military studies at Fort Warren in the 1950s (Denny, Wannamaker, Rammelkamp) showed that penicillin given for streptococcal pharyngitis substantially reduced rheumatic fever. That trial is the foundation of current antibiotic policy. Evidence of recent infection includes antistreptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers. Rheumatic heart disease is now rare in high-income countries but still causes major mortality in low-income settings.

**Fusobacterium necrophorum** is increasingly recognized in adolescent and young adult pharyngitis. In some studies its prevalence in 15 to 30 year olds rivals that of GAS. It is the classic cause of **Lemierre syndrome**: septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with septic emboli to the lungs. Because Centor-based strategies target only GAS, it remains debated whether this "other bacterial pharyngitis" warrants testing or treatment.

**Peritonsillar abscess anatomy and microbiology.** The **Weber glands**, minor salivary glands in the supratonsillar fossa, offer a competing explanation for PTA alongside the traditional view of tonsillitis spreading outward. This would explain why PTA occurs even after tonsillectomy. Cultures show mixed aerobes and anaerobes, with *F. necrophorum* and the *Streptococcus anginosus* group being common.

**Tonsil immunology.** The palatine tonsils are part of **Waldeyer's ring**, together with the adenoid, tubal and lingual tonsils. They are mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue with deep crypts lined by reticulated epithelium that contains M cells, which sample antigen into germinal centers. Immunological activity peaks in childhood, roughly between ages 3 and 10. Large cohort studies, such as a Danish registry analysis, found associations between childhood tonsillectomy and later respiratory and allergic disease. These findings are observational and confounded, so the long-term immune cost remains debated.
levels.expert:
**Guideline-based tonsillectomy.** The AAO-HNS clinical practice guideline (updated 2019) uses the **Paradise criteria** for recurrent throat infection: at least 7 documented episodes in the past year, at least 5 per year for 2 years, or at least 3 per year for 3 years. Each episode must be documented with fever, exudate, cervical adenopathy or a positive GAS test. Below these thresholds, **watchful waiting** is recommended, because Paradise's 1984 randomized trial showed benefit mainly in severely affected children, and that benefit faded over time. Other modifying factors include PFAPA syndrome (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis), multiple antibiotic allergies and a history of PTA. For **obstructive sleep-disordered breathing**, polysomnography is advised before surgery in children under 2 or with obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial anomalies, neuromuscular disease or sickle cell disease. The **CHAT trial** (2013) showed that adenotonsillectomy improved behavior, quality of life and polysomnographic findings, but not attention or executive function scores.

**Perioperative pearls.** Guidelines recommend a single intraoperative dose of dexamethasone and advise against routine perioperative antibiotics. **Codeine is contraindicated in children under 12** and after pediatric tonsillectomy, because ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers convert it into large amounts of morphine, and deaths from respiratory depression have occurred. This gives Odin a clear pharmacogenomic lesson. Ibuprofen is acceptable, since trials have not shown a clinically significant increase in bleeding. **Post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage** is either primary (within 24 hours, usually surgical technique) or secondary (typically days 5 to 10, when the eschar separates), occurring in a few percent of cases. Adults bleed more often than children. Intracapsular (partial) tonsillectomy lowers pain and bleeding risk but carries a small risk of regrowth.

**PTA pitfalls.** Before aspirating, remember that the internal carotid artery lies posterolateral to the tonsillar fossa. Keep the needle shallow and avoid going lateral. Intraoral or transcervical ultrasound improves diagnostic accuracy and reduces dry taps. CT is reserved for suspected extension into the parapharyngeal space or for an unclear diagnosis. Needle aspiration, incision and drainage, and quinsy ("hot") tonsillectomy have broadly similar success rates. Recurrence rates are around 10 to 15%, which is higher after a prior PTA.

**Open questions.** Should *F. necrophorum* testing become routine in adolescents? Is the Centor score still useful as rapid molecular GAS PCR spreads? Can the observational immune signals after tonsillectomy be confirmed by stronger causal study designs?

keyPoints: Most sore throats are viral; group A strep causes a minority, mainly in children 5-15
Centor/McIsaac criteria guide testing: fever, exudate, tender nodes, no cough
Treating strep with penicillin prevents rheumatic fever by eradicating GAS before the cross-reactive immune response develops
Peritonsillar abscess: trismus, hot-potato voice, uvula deviated away; drain plus antibiotics
Tonsillectomy indications: Paradise criteria for recurrent infection or sleep-disordered breathing
Codeine is contraindicated after pediatric tonsillectomy due to CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolism

test.q: What causes most cases of acute pharyngitis?
test.explain: Viruses such as rhinovirus and adenovirus cause most sore throats. Strep causes only a minority of cases.

test.q: Which finding counts toward the Centor score?
test.explain: Absence of cough is one of the four Centor points. Runny nose, hoarseness and red eyes point toward a virus.

test.q: A key reason to treat strep throat with antibiotics is to prevent:
test.explain: Antibiotics prevent acute rheumatic fever. They do not reliably prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

test.q: In a peritonsillar abscess, which way is the uvula pushed?
test.explain: The bulging abscess pushes the uvula toward the opposite side.

test.q: Trismus in peritonsillar abscess results from irritation of which muscle?
test.explain: Inflammation spreading to the nearby medial pterygoid muscle limits mouth opening.

test.q: Which virus causes mononucleosis, where amoxicillin often triggers a rash?
test.explain: EBV causes infectious mononucleosis, and amoxicillin given during it commonly produces a widespread rash.

test.q: Why is a negative rapid strep test in a child often backed up by culture?
choices: Culture is less costly to run
test.explain: Rapid antigen test sensitivity is imperfect, and children carry the highest risk of rheumatic fever.

test.q: Where does pus collect in a peritonsillar abscess?
choices: Under the floor of the mouth
test.explain: Pus collects between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle, usually at the upper pole.

test.q: Which drug is first line for group A strep pharyngitis?
test.explain: Penicillin or amoxicillin is first line, because GAS has no documented penicillin resistance.

test.q: Peritonsillar abscess is also known by the old name ___.
test.explain: Quinsy is the traditional name for peritonsillar abscess.

test.q: What is the name for difficulty opening the mouth?
test.explain: Trismus is a key sign that separates an abscess from simple tonsillitis.

test.q: Surgical removal of the palatine tonsils is called a ___.
test.explain: Tonsillectomy is often combined with adenoidectomy in children.

kidTest.q: What do tonsils do?
kidTest.explain: Tonsils are like guards that trap germs at the back of the mouth.

kidTest.q: What causes most sore throats?
kidTest.explain: Most sore throats come from viruses and get better on their own.

kidTest.q: How can a doctor check for strep?
kidTest.explain: A quick swab of the throat can find strep.

kidTest.q: What is a pocket of pus near a tonsil treated with?
kidTest.explain: Doctors drain the pus so it can heal.

kidTest.q: Sore throats can be caused by a germ called s _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Strep is the germ that doctors treat with medicine.

advancedTest.q: Why can PTA occur in a patient who has already had a tonsillectomy?
choices: Post-surgical scarring traps saliva produced by the parotid gland
Weber glands in the supratonsillar region can be the infection source
Lingual tonsil enlargement mimics a peritonsillar collection
Adenoid tissue regrows into the tonsillar fossa after surgery
advancedTest.explain: The Weber gland theory places the origin in minor salivary glands, which remain after the tonsils are removed.

advancedTest.q: A 19-year-old with a sore throat, a negative GAS test, and later neck vein thrombosis with lung nodules most likely had:
choices: Rheumatic fever caused by M protein mimicry
advancedTest.explain: F. necrophorum causes septic internal jugular thrombophlebitis with septic lung emboli, and GAS-focused testing misses it.

advancedTest.q: Why is codeine dangerous after pediatric tonsillectomy?
choices: It blocks dexamethasone and worsens throat swelling
It is converted to an inactive metabolite and fails
It inhibits platelets and greatly raises bleeding risk
Ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers make excess morphine
advancedTest.explain: Ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolism converts codeine into large amounts of morphine, causing fatal respiratory depression, especially in children with sleep apnea.

advancedTest.q: A child has had 4 documented strep throats in the past year. Per AAO-HNS guidance, the best plan is:
choices: Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis in place of surgery
Quinsy tonsillectomy during the next infection
Immediate tonsillectomy to prevent rheumatic fever
Watchful waiting, since Paradise thresholds are unmet
advancedTest.explain: The Paradise criteria require at least 7 episodes in 1 year, 5 per year for 2 years, or 3 per year for 3 years. Below that, watchful waiting is advised.

lessons.title: Deep Neck Infections, Epiglottitis and Stridor

levels.kid:
Your neck is like a busy hallway. Air goes down one tube to your lungs. Food goes down another tube to your tummy. Between them are soft layers, like blankets stacked together.

Sometimes germs sneak between those blankets and make a pocket of pus. That is called a **deep neck infection**. It can swell and squeeze the air tube.

The **epiglottis** is a little flap that covers your air tube when you swallow, like a lid on a cup. If it gets infected, it can puff up and block the air.

When air squeezes through a narrow tube, it makes a high, noisy sound called **stridor**. Stridor means "help, my airway is too small!" Doctors treat it as an emergency and keep the child calm.
levels.hs:
The neck contains layers of tissue called **fascia** that wrap muscles, organs and blood vessels. Between those layers are **potential spaces**: gaps that are normally closed but can fill with pus. A **deep neck infection** is an infection or abscess in one of these spaces, usually spreading from teeth, tonsils or the throat.

Important spaces:
- **Submandibular space** (under the jaw). Infection here, often from a lower molar, is called **Ludwig angina**. The floor of the mouth swells and pushes the tongue up and back.
- **Parapharyngeal space** (beside the throat).
- **Retropharyngeal space** (behind the throat), most common in young children.

**Epiglottitis** is infection and swelling of the epiglottis and nearby tissues (the "supraglottis"). It used to be caused mainly by *Haemophilus influenzae* type b (Hib). The Hib vaccine made it rare in children. Classic signs are the **four Ds**: drooling, dysphagia (trouble swallowing), dysphonia (muffled voice) and distress. Patients often sit leaning forward in the **tripod position**.

**Stridor** is a harsh, high-pitched breathing sound caused by turbulent airflow through a narrowed upper airway. Stridor heard when breathing in (**inspiratory**) usually points to a blockage at or above the vocal cords.

Example: a 6-year-old who is not vaccinated, has a high fever, drools and sits forward is treated as possible epiglottitis. Staff keep the child calm and avoid looking into the throat until the airway is secured.
levels.college:
**Fascial anatomy.** The deep cervical fascia has three layers: superficial (investing), middle (visceral/pretracheal) and deep (prevertebral). The spaces between them direct how infection spreads.
- **Retropharyngeal space**: between the visceral and alar fascia, from skull base to roughly T1-T2. It holds lymph nodes that shrink after about age 5, so abscesses here are mostly pediatric.
- **Danger space**: between the alar and prevertebral fascia. It runs down to the diaphragm, which gives a route to the mediastinum.
- **Parapharyngeal space**: an inverted pyramid beside the pharynx. Its poststyloid part contains the carotid sheath and cranial nerves IX-XII.
- **Submandibular space**: divided by the mylohyoid into sublingual and submaxillary parts. The roots of the second and third mandibular molars sit below the mylohyoid line, which explains why they cause Ludwig angina.

**Microbiology.** Most infections are polymicrobial: streptococci (viridans, *S. pyogenes*), *Staphylococcus aureus* (including MRSA) and oral anaerobes such as *Prevotella* and *Fusobacterium*.

**Diagnosis.** Contrast-enhanced CT is the workhorse. An abscess appears as a low-density collection with rim enhancement. A lateral neck X-ray can show prevertebral widening.

**Management principles:**
- Airway first. Patients may need awake fiberoptic intubation or a surgical airway.
- IV antibiotics that cover streptococci, staphylococci and anaerobes.
- Surgical or needle drainage for mature abscesses. Small pediatric retropharyngeal collections often respond to antibiotics alone.

**Epiglottitis** today is more common in adults and has more varied causes (streptococci, *S. aureus*, non-type-b *H. influenzae*). A lateral X-ray can show the **thumbprint sign**. In stable adults, flexible nasolaryngoscopy confirms the diagnosis.

**Stridor localization:**
- Inspiratory: supraglottic or glottic level (epiglottitis, laryngomalacia).
- Biphasic: glottic or subglottic level (croup, subglottic stenosis).
- Expiratory: intrathoracic trachea or bronchi.

**Croup** (viral laryngotracheobronchitis, mainly parainfluenza) causes a barking cough and the **steeple sign** on a frontal X-ray. The child is usually not toxic and not drooling, which separates croup from epiglottitis and bacterial tracheitis.
levels.phd:
**Airflow physics.** Laminar resistance follows Poiseuille's law: resistance scales with 1/r^4. If 1 mm of mucosal edema narrows an infant's subglottis from about 4 mm to 2 mm in diameter, resistance rises roughly 16-fold. Once flow becomes turbulent, pressure drop depends on flow squared and gas density. This is the rationale for **heliox**: its lower density reduces turbulent resistance, buying time but not treating the cause. The extrathoracic airway narrows during inspiration because intraluminal pressure falls below atmospheric pressure. That dynamic collapse explains why upper airway lesions produce inspiratory stridor, while intrathoracic lesions, held open by negative pleural pressure on inspiration, become noisy during expiration.

**The Hib natural experiment.** Before conjugate Hib vaccines arrived in the late 1980s and early 1990s, pediatric epiglottitis was a classic disease of children aged 2-7. Incidence then fell by well over 90% in children, and the median age shifted into adulthood. Adult disease follows a slower course, with sore throat and odynophagia out of proportion to the oropharyngeal exam. Persistent pediatric cases involve vaccine failure, other serotypes, *Streptococcus*, *Staphylococcus* or *Candida* in immunocompromised hosts. Thermal and caustic injury can mimic infection.

**Lemierre syndrome.** This is septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein after pharyngeal infection, classically caused by *Fusobacterium necrophorum*, with septic pulmonary emboli. It shows how parapharyngeal infection reaches the carotid sheath. Other vascular complications include carotid pseudoaneurysm and "herald bleeds."

**Descending necrotizing mediastinitis.** Spread through the retropharyngeal or danger space follows gravity and negative intrathoracic pressure into the mediastinum. Historical mortality was 25-40%. Estrera's criteria (1983) defined the condition. Outcomes improved with aggressive transcervical plus transthoracic drainage guided by CT extent.

**Controversies.** One debate is whether CT "abscess" equals drainable pus. Contrast CT has a meaningful false-positive rate: phlegmon can show rim enhancement. Pediatric series show that many children with small retropharyngeal collections (often under about 2 cm) recover with antibiotics alone. The use of corticosteroids in deep neck infection and adult epiglottitis remains debated, and randomized data are limited.
levels.expert:
**Airway decision-making is the core skill.** In a patient with a threatened airway, the question is not "what is the diagnosis" but "where, how and by whom will this airway be secured." Practical principles:
- Do not lie a patient with suspected supraglottic obstruction flat. Do not send an unstable patient to the CT scanner. Do not attempt tongue-depressor exams on a distressed child.
- The preferred setting is the operating room, with anesthesia and an ENT surgeon scrubbed and a tracheostomy or cricothyrotomy kit opened.
- **Awake fiberoptic intubation** keeps spontaneous breathing. Muscle relaxants given to a patient with a supraglottic mass can convert a "can ventilate" situation into **cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate** (CICO).
- In Ludwig angina, trismus and floor-of-mouth swelling may make the oral route impossible. Awake tracheostomy under local anesthesia remains a legitimate first-line choice.
- In pediatric cricothyroid anatomy, surgical cricothyrotomy is generally avoided in young children (roughly under 10-12 years). Needle cricothyroidotomy or rigid bronchoscopy is preferred.

**Pitfalls.**
- **Diabetes** is the strongest host risk factor for complicated deep neck infection, with more multispace disease, *Klebsiella pneumoniae* and longer stays. Check glucose.
- A falling or absent fever after starting antibiotics does not exclude a collection. Reimage when a patient fails to improve in 48-72 hours.
- Neck stiffness and torticollis in a child can come from retropharyngeal abscess and be mistaken for meningitis.
- Horner syndrome or lower cranial neuropathies point to poststyloid parapharyngeal involvement.
- Stridor in an infant is usually **laryngomalacia**, but persistent or worsening stridor needs endoscopy for subglottic stenosis, hemangioma or vocal fold paralysis. A vocal fold paralysis workup may lead to a neurosurgical lesion such as Chiari malformation.

**Recent advances and open questions.** Image-guided transoral or ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is reducing open drainage in selected cases. Rising rates of community MRSA and clindamycin resistance are shifting empiric choices. Video laryngoscopy and high-flow nasal oxygen, used to extend apnoeic time, have changed airway rescue planning. Unanswered questions include which small abscesses can be safely managed without drainage, and whether early steroids shorten the course without masking deterioration.

keyPoints: Deep neck infections spread through potential spaces between layers of deep cervical fascia
Ludwig angina is a submandibular space infection, usually from lower molars
The danger space connects the neck to the mediastinum
Epiglottitis: drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice, tripod position; now mostly adults after Hib vaccine
Inspiratory stridor suggests obstruction at or above the vocal cords
Secure the airway first, in a controlled setting, before imaging or examining the throat

test.q: Ludwig angina is an infection of which neck space?
test.explain: Ludwig angina involves the submandibular space, usually spreading from lower molar teeth. It pushes the tongue up and back.

test.q: Why is retropharyngeal abscess mainly a disease of young children?
choices: Their tonsils are located lower in the neck
Their lymph nodes there shrink after about age 5
Their fascia layers have not yet formed
Their teeth are more prone to decay
test.explain: The retropharyngeal lymph nodes regress after about age 5, so suppurative nodes and abscesses here are mostly pediatric.

test.q: Which space offers a route for infection to reach the mediastinum?
test.explain: The danger space lies between alar and prevertebral fascia and extends down to the diaphragm.

test.q: Which vaccine made pediatric epiglottitis rare?
test.explain: Haemophilus influenzae type b was the classic cause; the conjugate Hib vaccine dramatically reduced childhood cases.

test.q: A child with epiglottitis typically sits:
choices: Reclined with the head tilted back
Leaning forward in a tripod position
test.explain: Leaning forward in the tripod position helps keep the narrowed airway open.

test.q: Inspiratory stridor most likely points to narrowing at which level?
choices: At or above the vocal cords
test.explain: The extrathoracic airway narrows on inspiration, so supraglottic or glottic lesions give inspiratory stridor. Intrathoracic lesions are louder on expiration.

test.q: What imaging test is the main tool for diagnosing a deep neck abscess?
test.explain: Contrast CT shows a low-density collection with rim enhancement and maps how far infection has spread.

test.q: Which feature best separates croup from epiglottitis?
test.explain: Croup gives a barking cough in a non-toxic child who is not drooling. Fever and stridor can occur in both.

test.q: Most deep neck infections are caused by:
test.explain: They are usually polymicrobial: streptococci, staphylococci and oral anaerobes. Candida matters mainly in immunocompromised hosts.

test.q: What is the name of the harsh, high-pitched breathing sound caused by upper airway narrowing?
test.explain: Stridor results from turbulent airflow through a narrowed upper airway.

test.q: On a lateral neck X-ray, a swollen epiglottis can produce the ___ sign.
test.explain: The swollen epiglottis looks like a thumbprint on a lateral view.

test.q: Croup can show the ___ sign on a frontal neck X-ray.
test.explain: Subglottic narrowing tapers the air column like a church steeple.

kidTest.q: What does the epiglottis do?
choices: Covers the air tube when you swallow
kidTest.explain: It is a little lid that keeps food out of the air tube.

kidTest.q: What is stridor?
choices: A clicking sound from the jaw
A noisy sound from a narrow air tube
A soft sound from a full tummy
kidTest.explain: Stridor is a high, noisy sound when air squeezes through a tight airway.

kidTest.q: What can form between the neck's soft layers when germs get in?
kidTest.explain: Germs can make a pocket of pus, called a deep neck infection.

kidTest.q: What do doctors do for a child with stridor?
choices: Ask the child to lie flat and wait
kidTest.explain: Staying calm helps the child breathe while doctors protect the airway.

kidTest.q: The neck has soft layers stacked like b _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The tissue layers are like stacked blankets with gaps between them.

advancedTest.q: Mucosal edema halves the radius of an infant's subglottis. Under laminar flow, resistance rises about:
advancedTest.explain: Poiseuille's law makes resistance scale with 1/r^4, so halving radius raises resistance about 16-fold.

advancedTest.q: Why can paralytic drugs be dangerous when intubating a patient with supraglottic obstruction?
choices: They block the antibiotics used against anaerobes
They raise blood pressure and worsen local bleeding
They speed spread of infection into the mediastinum
Loss of muscle tone can turn a ventilatable airway into CICO
advancedTest.explain: Spontaneous breathing and tone help keep the airway patent; abolishing them risks a cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate crisis, which is why awake fiberoptic intubation is favored.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a parapharyngeal infection develops Horner syndrome. This most strongly suggests:
choices: An isolated dental abscess above the mylohyoid line
Involvement of the poststyloid compartment near the carotid sheath
Spread confined to the sublingual part of the submandibular space
Simple viral croup causing subglottic swelling
advancedTest.explain: The poststyloid parapharyngeal space contains the carotid sheath and sympathetic chain plus cranial nerves IX-XII, so their dysfunction localizes there.

advancedTest.q: Heliox helps a patient with critical upper airway narrowing mainly because it:
choices: Has low density, easing turbulent flow
Reduces mucosal swelling of the airway directly
Kills bacteria growing in the airway wall
Raises oxygen content well above room air
advancedTest.explain: Turbulent pressure drop depends on gas density; heliox's low density lowers resistance and buys time without treating the cause.

lessons.title: Hoarseness, Vocal Fold Lesions and Laryngeal Cancer

levels.kid:
Put your fingers on the front of your neck and hum. Feel the buzz? That buzz comes from your **voice box**. Inside it are two soft folds that wiggle together very fast when you talk, like the lips of a balloon squeaking when you stretch the neck.

When the folds get swollen or bumpy, your voice sounds rough and scratchy. That is called being **hoarse**. A cold or a lot of yelling at a game can do it, and it usually gets better in a few days.

If you yell a lot for a long time, little bumps like calluses can grow on the folds. Resting your voice helps.

If a grown-up's voice stays rough for weeks, a doctor looks inside with a tiny camera to check that nothing serious is growing.
levels.hs:
**Hoarseness** (doctors also call it **dysphonia**) means a rough, breathy, strained or weak voice. Voice is made in the **larynx** (voice box). Air from the lungs passes between two **vocal folds**, which vibrate hundreds of times per second to make sound. Anything that stops the folds from closing evenly or vibrating smoothly changes the voice.

Common causes:
- **Acute laryngitis**: swelling from a cold virus or from shouting. It usually clears in 1 to 2 weeks.
- **Vocal fold nodules**: callus-like bumps on both folds, caused by repeated voice overuse. They are common in teachers, singers and children who shout a lot.
- **Polyps**: usually a single soft lump, sometimes after one episode of shouting.
- **Vocal fold paralysis**: the nerve that moves a fold is damaged, for example during thyroid surgery.
- **Laryngeal cancer**: most often linked to smoking and heavy alcohol use.

Doctors look at the folds with a **laryngoscope**, a thin camera passed through the nose. Guidelines advise this when hoarseness lasts more than about 4 weeks, or sooner if there are warning signs.

Real example: a smoker in his 60s with hoarseness for 6 weeks needs his larynx examined. In the vocal folds, a cancer often causes hoarseness early, while the tumor is still small. That gives doctors a good chance to find it at an early stage.
levels.college:
The larynx has three regions: the **supraglottis** (epiglottis, false folds), the **glottis** (true vocal folds) and the **subglottis**. Voice comes from the **mucosal wave**: air pressure from below opens the closed folds, and elastic recoil plus the Bernoulli effect pull them shut again. This wave depends on a loose, jelly-like layer just under the surface called **Reinke's space** (the superficial lamina propria).

**Nerve supply.** The **recurrent laryngeal nerve** (RLN), a branch of the vagus, supplies all the intrinsic muscles except the cricothyroid. The left RLN loops under the aortic arch, so it is longer and more easily injured. Causes of injury include thyroid surgery, lung cancer, an aortic aneurysm and mediastinal tumors.

**Benign lesions:**
- **Nodules**: on both folds, at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds, where impact is greatest. First-line treatment is voice therapy.
- **Polyps**: usually one-sided, often hemorrhagic. They may need microsurgery.
- **Reinke's edema**: diffuse, fluid-filled swelling of Reinke's space, strongly linked to smoking. It causes a deep, low voice.
- **Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis**: wart-like growths caused by HPV types 6 and 11.
- **Laryngopharyngeal reflux** can contribute to irritation.

**Laryngeal cancer.** About 95% are **squamous cell carcinomas**. The main risk factors are tobacco and alcohol, which act synergistically. Glottic tumors are the most common subsite in many countries. They cause hoarseness early and spread to lymph nodes late, because the true folds have very few lymphatics. Supraglottic tumors come to attention later, and many have already spread to nodes.

**Red flags:** hoarseness in a smoker, **stridor**, pain on swallowing, ear pain referred through the vagus nerve, a neck lump, coughing up blood, and weight loss.
levels.phd:
The **body-cover model** (Hirano) describes the fold as layers. The cover is the epithelium plus the superficial lamina propria (SLP). The transition layer is the vocal ligament, formed by the intermediate and deep lamina propria. The body is the thyroarytenoid (vocalis) muscle. Normal vibration needs the cover to move freely over the body. Scarring of the SLP or a sulcus vocalis stiffens the cover and damps the mucosal wave, and this is a hard problem to fix. **Videostroboscopy** shows the wave as apparent slow motion, using pulses of light synced to the frequency of vibration. It reveals stiff segments that ordinary laryngoscopy misses.

Nodules correspond to areas of high collision stress, which is why they form in matched pairs. Their tissue shows SLP edema and fibronectin deposits. Polyps show vascular and gelatinous changes. In papillomatosis, the HPV6/11 E6 and E7 proteins drive epithelial growth. However, low-risk HPV types rarely cause cancer, and they are distinct from the HPV16 that drives oropharyngeal cancer.

**Carcinogenesis** progresses along a sequence: hyperplasia, then keratosis, dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, and finally invasive SCC. Tumors share field-cancerization changes with other smoking-related SCC, including TP53 mutation, CDKN2A loss and EGFR overexpression. HPV plays a small, debated role in the larynx, unlike in the oropharynx.

**Barriers to spread** are clinically important. These include Broyles' ligament at the anterior commissure, the thyroid cartilage, and the paraglottic and pre-epiglottic spaces. In AJCC TNM staging, fixation of the vocal fold upgrades a glottic tumor to T3. Fixation can come from invasion of the paraglottic space or the arytenoid.

**The organ preservation era.** The 1991 VA Larynx Trial found that induction chemotherapy followed by radiation preserved the larynx in about two-thirds of patients without hurting survival. RTOG 91-11 then showed that concurrent chemoradiation gave the best larynx preservation. Long-term follow-up raised a debate about non-cancer deaths with concurrent therapy. Population data from the US have also linked the shift away from laryngectomy to worse survival in advanced (T4) disease. This prompted the guideline that T4a tumors with cartilage destruction generally go to primary surgery.
levels.expert:
**Workup in practice.** AAO-HNS guidance says a clinician should not routinely give antibiotics, corticosteroids or anti-reflux medication for hoarseness before the larynx has been seen. Empiric reflux treatment without findings is a common reason diagnoses are delayed. Imaging is reserved for patients whose larynx has already been examined.

For unilateral paralysis, image the whole course of the vagus and RLN, from the skull base to the aortic arch. The scan is CT from the skull base to the mediastinum. A neurosurgery link: jugular foramen lesions such as paragangliomas or schwannomas can cause a high vagal palsy alongside CN IX and XI deficits (Vernet syndrome).

**Paralysis management.** Injection laryngoplasty, a temporary augmentation, restores closure while awaiting recovery. Early injection may reduce the need for later permanent surgery. Permanent options include medialization thyroplasty (Isshiki type I) and laryngeal reinnervation (ansa cervicalis to RLN). Continuous intraoperative nerve monitoring during thyroidectomy reduces the risk of bilateral palsy.

**Early glottic cancer (T1–T2).** Transoral laser microsurgery and radiotherapy give similar local control. The choice turns on voice outcome, involvement of the anterior commissure and the patient's own priorities. Radiotherapy alone also allows salvage later.

**Advanced disease.** Total laryngectomy separates the airway from the food passage, leaving a permanent tracheostoma. Voice is restored with a **tracheoesophageal puncture prosthesis** or an electrolarynx. A key pitfall: a laryngectomee breathes only through the neck stoma. Oxygen and ventilation must go to the stoma, not the mouth.

After salvage surgery for failed chemoradiation, fistula rates are high, which is why vascularized flaps are used. Surveillance is hard because of radiation changes, and PET-CT at about 12 weeks has a high negative predictive value.

**Frontiers:**
- **Bevacizumab** in papillomatosis, given systemically or into the lesion.
- **HPV vaccination**, expected to reduce papillomatosis by blocking mother-to-infant transmission.
- **Checkpoint inhibitors** such as pembrolizumab, for recurrent or metastatic SCC with high PD-L1 CPS.
- **Larynx-preservation selection** using induction response.
- **Tissue engineering** of the SLP for vocal fold scar.

keyPoints: Hoarseness (dysphonia) arises when the vocal folds cannot close or vibrate evenly
Laryngoscopy is advised for hoarseness lasting beyond about 4 weeks or with red flags
Nodules are bilateral and from overuse; first-line treatment is voice therapy
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch and is easily injured
About 95% of laryngeal cancers are squamous cell carcinoma linked to tobacco and alcohol
Glottic cancer causes early hoarseness and rarely spreads to nodes early

test.q: Bilateral callus-like lesions in a teacher who overuses her voice are most likely:
test.explain: Nodules are paired lesions from repeated phonotrauma. Polyps are usually unilateral.

test.q: Why is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve more often injured than the right?
choices: It runs inside the thyroid gland
It lacks a protective myelin sheath
It loops under the aortic arch
It leaves the skull through the orbit
test.explain: The left RLN takes a long course around the aortic arch, exposing it to chest disease and surgery.

test.q: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is NOT supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
test.explain: The cricothyroid is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

test.q: What is the most common histological type of laryngeal cancer?
test.explain: About 95% of laryngeal cancers are squamous cell carcinomas arising from the lining epithelium.

test.q: Why are glottic cancers often caught at an early stage?
choices: They cause pain long before growing
They are visible on the outer neck
They raise a reliable blood marker
test.explain: Even a small tumor on the vibrating fold changes the voice, so patients come to attention early.

test.q: Diffuse swelling of Reinke's space with a deepened voice is most linked to:
test.explain: Reinke's edema is strongly associated with smoking.

test.q: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis is caused by:
test.explain: Low-risk HPV 6 and 11 cause the wart-like growths. HPV16 is linked to oropharyngeal cancer instead.

test.q: Which symptom in a hoarse smoker is a red flag for cancer?
choices: Voice tiredness after a long talk
test.explain: Referred otalgia via the vagus nerve, together with painful swallowing, suggests a deeper tumor.

test.q: What is the first-line treatment for vocal fold nodules?
test.explain: Nodules usually shrink with voice therapy that corrects phonotrauma. Surgery is rarely needed.

test.q: The medical term for hoarseness or impaired voice is ___.
test.explain: Dysphonia covers rough, breathy, strained or weak voice.

test.q: What is the instrument or camera used to look at the vocal folds called?
test.explain: A flexible laryngoscope is passed through the nose to view the larynx.

test.q: The true vocal folds form the region of the larynx called the ___.
test.explain: The larynx is divided into supraglottis, glottis and subglottis.

kidTest.q: Where in your body is your voice made?
kidTest.explain: The voice box in your neck holds the folds that buzz.

kidTest.q: What does 'hoarse' mean?
kidTest.explain: Hoarse means a scratchy, rough voice.

kidTest.q: What can make little bumps grow on the vocal folds?
choices: Yelling a lot for a long time
kidTest.explain: Lots of yelling rubs the folds and makes callus-like bumps.

kidTest.q: What helps a sore, tired voice get better?
kidTest.explain: Voice rest lets the folds heal.

kidTest.q: Doctors look inside with a tiny c _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A tiny camera lets the doctor see the voice box.

advancedTest.q: A singer has normal-looking folds on laryngoscopy but a persistent poor voice. Why might videostroboscopy help?
choices: It measures airflow resistance across the subglottis directly
It reveals stiff segments that damp the mucosal wave
It detects HPV DNA within the vocal fold epithelium
It images the recurrent laryngeal nerve course in the chest
advancedTest.explain: Stroboscopy shows the vibration of the cover layer. Scar or sulcus stiffens the cover and damps the wave even when the fold looks normal.

advancedTest.q: Supraglottic cancers present with nodal disease more often than glottic cancers mainly because:
choices: Supraglottic tumors grow from cartilage cells
The supraglottis has rich lymphatic drainage
The glottis lies largely outside the larynx
advancedTest.explain: The true folds have sparse lymphatics, while the supraglottis drains richly to the neck, so it presents late with nodes.

advancedTest.q: Why are T4a laryngeal tumors with cartilage destruction generally treated with primary surgery?
choices: Radiation is unable to reach tumors located in the glottis
The shift from laryngectomy was linked to worse survival in this group
Chemoradiation was rarely tested in advanced laryngeal stages
Surgery reliably preserves natural voice in T4a tumors
advancedTest.explain: US population data associated declining laryngectomy with worse survival in advanced disease, so cartilage-destroying tumors favor total laryngectomy.

advancedTest.q: A patient with unilateral fold paralysis also has weak shoulder shrug and impaired gag. Where is the lesion most likely?
choices: Along the left RLN beneath the aortic arch
advancedTest.explain: Combined CN IX, X and XI deficits point to the jugular foramen (Vernet syndrome), not a distal RLN injury.
